problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as loading probability distributions into quantum states so that the quantum expectation estimation algorithm can be used for Monte Carlo-style expectation estimation in finance. It focuses on making qGAN-based distribution loading work efficiently in shallow circuits, especially for distributions such as the log-normal distribution used in financial engineering.
problem_statement_quotes: Since quantum computers can utilize a fast expectation estimation algorithm, known as the quantum expectation estimation algorithm, it is expected that the algorithm can be used instead of the Monte Carlo method in classical computers to speed up expectation estimation [3–5].
Executing the quantum expectation estimation algorithm needs the construction of a quantum circuit capable of loading a probability distribution into a quantum state.

We demonstrate that our proposed method can generate the log-normal distribution, which is pivotal in ﬁnancial engineering, as well as the triangular distribution and the bimodal distribution, more eﬃciently than current methods.
classical_baseline: The paper treats Monte Carlo simulation on classical computers as the baseline for expectation estimation, and Grover-Rudolph state preparation as the classical/standard state-preparation approach for loading distributions. It also compares against prior qGAN initializations such as the uniform distribution and the normal distribution.
classical_baseline_quotes: Monte Carlo-based expectation estimation using a classical computer requires O(1/ǫ2) number of simulations for the desired accuracy ǫ.
One method is the Grover-Rudolph state preparation [11], but it requires up to O(2n) gates and quantum circuit depth, making it diﬃcult to use in NISQ devices.
In this study, the initial distribution was our initial distribution, the uniform distribution, and the normal distribution with a mean and standard deviation of the target probability distribution.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical Monte Carlo method needs O(1/ǫ2) simulations for a target accuracy, while the quantum expectation estimation algorithm needs only O(1/ǫ) oracle queries. For state preparation, Grover-Rudolph requires up to O(2n) gates and circuit depth, and the normal-distribution initialization for qGANs may require deeper circuits as qubit count grows, which can remove the shallow-circuit advantage.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Monte Carlo-based expectation estimation using a classical computer requires O(1/ǫ2) number of simulations for the desired accuracy ǫ.
In contrast, the quantum expectation estimation algorithm, which uses an amplitude estimation algorithm, is known to be able to estimate an expectation in O(1/ǫ) oracle queries [3].
One method is the Grover-Rudolph state preparation [11], but it requires up to O(2n) gates and quantum circuit depth, making it diﬃcult to use in NISQ devices.

However, as the number of qubits increases, a deeper quantum circuit is considered necessary to generate a normal distribution. Therefore, qGANs using the normal distribution for the initial distribution may lose the advantage of shallow circuit depth, a feature of circuit generation using qGANs.
business_stakes: The paper explicitly ties the motivation to financial engineering and to speeding up expectation estimation for finance-related Monte Carlo methods. It also says the log-normal distribution is pivotal in financial engineering.
business_stakes_quotes: one example is the quantum expectation estimation algorithm that accelerates the widely-used Monte Carlo method in ﬁelds such as ﬁnance.

Since quantum computers can utilize a fast expectation estimation algorithm, known as the quantum expectation estimation algorithm, it is expected that the algorithm can be used instead of the Monte Carlo method in classical computers to speed up expectation estimation [3–5].

We demonstrate that our proposed method can generate the log-normal distribution, which is pivotal in ﬁnancial engineering, as well as the triangular distribution and the bimodal distribution, more eﬃciently than current methods.
